content.intro: Learn url, view, and template errors through a compact visual, an inspectable Django example, and a practical verification task.
content.why_it_matters: URL, View, and Template Errors matters because a Django project has to behave predictably across requests, database state, configuration, and deployments. Understanding this piece makes the surrounding application easier to test, maintain, and secure.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: This lesson examines url, view, and template errors as part of troubleshooting and legacy compatibility. The objective is to understand the behavior, connect it to the listed subtopics, and verify it with a small example rather than relying on memorized syntax.

content_blocks.title: What to cover
content_blocks.text: The source syllabus for this lesson names: URL pattern mismatches; Reverse-resolution errors; Missing templates; Incorrect context data; Unexpected response status codes. Keep these distinct concepts together: know what each item does, when it applies, and what assumption must be verified in your project.

items.title: URL pattern mismatches
items.text: URL pattern mismatches is part of the request/response contract. Match routes and methods explicitly, return an appropriate response/status, and test success, missing-resource and unauthorized paths.

items.title: Reverse-resolution errors
items.text: Treat Reverse-resolution errors as a reproducible diagnostic: capture the exact input and observed result, isolate one hypothesis, and add a regression test once the cause is fixed. Avoid exposing internal stack traces or secrets to public users.

items.title: Missing templates
items.text: Missing templates shapes the presentation layer. Separate layout from business logic, escape untrusted output, provide meaningful empty/error states, and check semantic structure and keyboard usability.

items.title: Incorrect context data
items.text: Incorrect context data affects persistence and data correctness. Keep invariants in validation and database constraints where appropriate, inspect generated SQL/migrations, and test both expected data and error/rollback behavior.

items.title: Unexpected response status codes
items.text: Unexpected response status codes is part of the request/response contract. Match routes and methods explicitly, return an appropriate response/status, and test success, missing-resource and unauthorized paths.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: URL, View, and Template Errors
content_blocks.code:
from django.urls import path
from . import views

urlpatterns = [
    path("items/<int:item_id>/", views.item_detail, name="item-detail"),
]
content_blocks.expected_output: The route converter passes an integer item_id to the named view.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Open a local project using the documented Django 6.1-compatible Python environment. If this snippet depends on model names, URL configuration, settings, or an optional package, add those prerequisites before running it. Otherwise inspect it as a static example. CodeLeaf browser preview does not execute Django/Python server code.
content_blocks.troubleshooting: The view and project include() wiring must exist; URL conversion does not perform authorization or database lookup.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: Common pitfalls include skipping a required configuration/import, copying a fragment without its model or URL context, trusting client input, or treating a development-only behavior as production-ready. Check the earliest failing assumption, consult the version-specific docs, and add a regression test for the failure you found.
